findings.problem: The auxiliary fact `composition` says that restriction is functorial, up to reassociating composites. The proof is a three-step `calc` that threads `Category.assoc` and `restriction.map_comp` through hand-written `congrArg (fun morphism => ...)` lambdas. Most of its 12 lines are bookkeeping for where each rewrite applies, which hides the single idea: `restriction.map (s ≫ g.hom) = restriction.map s ≫ restriction.map g.hom`. Every morphism in the statement uses only the local names `unitIso`, `restriction`, `s`, `g`, `f`, so plain syntactic rewriting is enough.
findings.proposed_change:
Replace lines 39–47 (the whole `calc` block) with the standard idiom:

```lean
  have composition :
      (unitIso.inv ≫ restriction.map s) ≫ restriction.map g.hom ≫ f.hom =
        (unitIso.inv ≫ restriction.map (s ≫ g.hom)) ≫ f.hom := by
    simp only [Functor.map_comp, Category.assoc]
```

This splits `restriction.map (s ≫ g.hom)` with `Functor.map_comp` and right-associates both sides with `Category.assoc`, after which they are syntactically equal.
findings.benefit: The proof now names its two ingredients directly: functoriality (`Functor.map_comp`) and associativity (`Category.assoc`). The reader no longer has to work through nested `congrArg` lambdas and `.trans`/`.symm` chains to see that nothing else is involved. It is a common Mathlib idiom, it is not opaque automation (a `simp only` with two named lemmas), and it removes about ten lines of noise without hiding any mathematical step.

evidence.excerpt: map_comp : ∀ {X Y Z : C} (f : X ⟶ Y) (g : Y ⟶ Z), map (f ≫ g) = map f ≫ map g := by cat_disch

_ = unitIso.inv ≫ restriction.map (s ≫ g.hom) ≫ f.hom :=
        congrArg (fun morphism => unitIso.inv ≫ morphism ≫ f.hom)
